# Performance Marketing Is Not a Channel. It Is a Way of Paying.

Source: https://lowob.com/research/performance-marketing-way-of-paying/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-06-06 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Distribution

> Summary: Performance marketing is a way of paying, not a channel. The company pays when something happens, an account opened, a subscription started, a qualified lead delivered, rather than when something is shown. It only works when three conditions hold: the outcome is observable in the company's own tracking, attributable with enough confidence to pay against, and worth the payment over a realistic horizon. If any of the three fails, the company is not paying for performance. It is paying for a story about performance.

## Key points

- Performance marketing is a payment standard: pay per defined outcome, not per impression.
- It applies across creators, affiliates, programmatic buys optimised to cost per acquisition and revenue-share partners.
- Last-click payment rewards whoever touches the customer last; creators' lawsuits against PayPal's Honey extension allege exactly that leak.
- Four weekly numbers are enough: cost per qualified outcome, approval rate, payback and concentration.
- Some things that matter, such as trust in a financial product, move the outcome numbers without ever appearing in them.

Ask three people what performance marketing is and you will get three answers. To one, it is the paid-social team. To another, it is affiliate. To the third, it is anything with a dashboard. All three are describing a channel. None of them is describing the idea.

Performance marketing is a way of paying. Everything else is a mechanism for making that payment possible. The definition matters because it travels. It applies to a creator paid per activated account, an affiliate paid per approved application, a programmatic buy optimised to cost per acquisition, and a partner paid a revenue share. It also makes clear where a programme stops being performance marketing and becomes exposure with a spreadsheet attached.

## The three conditions

A channel can be run on performance terms only if three conditions hold.

**The outcome is observable.** The company can see, with its own tracking, that the paid-for event occurred. Not the partner's report of it. Its own. This has become harder: Apple's App Tracking Transparency rules mean an app user who declines tracking shows an advertising identifier of all zeros, and browsers block much cross-site tracking. Our piece on [how marketing tracking works](https://lowob.com/research/how-marketing-tracking-works/) covers the first-party and server-side setup that keeps outcomes observable.

**The outcome is attributable.** The company can connect the event to the source that produced it with enough confidence to pay against it. This is where most programmes quietly break. Last-click attribution pays whoever touched the customer last, which rewards coupon sites and browser extensions that appeared at checkout after the actual persuasion happened elsewhere.

**The outcome is worth the payment.** A cost per acquisition is only a number until it is compared with what an acquired customer is worth over a realistic horizon, net of refunds, fraud and churn. Performance programmes with generous payouts and loose definitions are a machine for buying customers who leave. Our explainer on [CAC payback](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-cac-payback/) covers the calculation.

| Condition | The test | Where it usually fails | The fix |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Observable | Does our own tracking record the event? | Partner reports only; app tracking declined | First-party events, server-side, unique codes |
| Attributable | Can we tie it to the source with confidence? | Last click credits the checkout touch | Stand-down rules, holdouts, payment on approved outcomes |
| Worth it | Does value over the horizon exceed the payout? | Loose definitions, early churn | Written definition, clawback window, payback limit |

## Where last-click payment leaks

The attribution failure is not hypothetical. In late 2024 and early 2025, content creators filed class actions alleging that PayPal's Honey browser extension replaced their affiliate cookies with its own at checkout, taking commission for sales the creators had referred. The complaint alleges Honey was built to avoid "standing down" for ordinary shoppers while complying when it suspected it was being tested. In June 2026 a federal judge denied PayPal's renewed motion to dismiss, sending the case to discovery. That is not a finding of liability; PayPal disputes the claims. It does show how a last-click payment rule can be captured by whoever sits closest to the checkout.

The same pattern appears in paid search. When eBay switched off its brand keyword ads in a field experiment, about 99.5% of the click traffic arrived anyway through organic search. A performance programme paying per click on the company's own brand name would have paid for customers it already had.

The remedy is not to abandon performance terms. It is to pay on outcomes the company has approved, to require stand-down from coupon and cashback partners when another partner referred the visit, and to test the biggest partners with holdouts. Our piece on [referral partners without leakage](https://lowob.com/research/referral-partners-without-leakage/) covers the registration and protection rules, and [attribution versus incrementality](https://lowob.com/research/attribution-vs-incrementality/) covers the holdout designs.

> If the outcome is not observable, attributable and worth the payment, the company is not paying for performance. It is paying for a story about performance.

## Performance terms for a company the platforms restrict

For fintech, AI and other reviewed categories, the performance question is sharper, because the channels most companies default to may not be available at all.

That turns out to be a useful constraint. The open-band channels, affiliate, creator, clipping, programmatic against defined audiences, are the ones that most naturally accept performance terms. A creator will accept a cost-per-account deal when the product converts. An affiliate network runs on it. A programmatic partner can be paid on a flat fee while the buy itself is optimised to cost per outcome.

The company that cannot buy the crowded auction is pushed toward the channels where paying for outcomes is normal. That is a better place to start than most companies realise. Our piece on [distribution when ad platforms restrict you](https://lowob.com/research/distribution-when-ad-platforms-restrict-you/) covers the channel map.

## The four numbers to keep

Skip the twenty-tab report. Four figures, tracked weekly, are enough to run a performance programme without fooling anyone.

| Number | Definition | What it tells you | Warning sign |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cost per qualified outcome | Total payout divided by outcomes meeting the written definition | What the programme really costs | Definition changed mid-quarter |
| Approval rate | Share of reported outcomes the company's own tracking confirms and accepts | Fraud and quality | A widening gap between reported and approved |
| Payback | Months of realistic customer value to recover the acquisition cost | Whether the price is affordable | Payback lengthening as volume grows |
| Concentration | Share of outcomes from the top three partners or placements | Dependency risk | Above half: one relationship, not a channel |

"Qualified" should be defined in writing and held fixed for the quarter. A definition that moves is the easiest way to make a programme look better than it is.

## Where performance marketing stops being true

Two honest limits.

Performance terms push risk onto the partner, and partners price that risk in. A creator paid per account will ask for more per account than the equivalent flat fee, and will drop the product if it does not convert. That is a fair trade, but it is a trade.

And some things that matter cannot be paid for per outcome. Trust in a financial product, comprehension of a new category, a founder's reputation in a market: these move the outcome numbers without ever appearing in them. The research on advertising effectiveness supports the point. Binet and Field's analysis of IPA effectiveness cases found brand effects decay slowly and build over years, while activation effects are large and short; in their B2B work the best-performing balance was 46% brand and 54% activation. A performance programme that starves the slow work will see its cost per outcome rise for reasons the dashboard cannot explain. Our piece on [brand versus performance marketing](https://lowob.com/research/brand-vs-performance-marketing/) covers the split.

Performance marketing is a payment standard, not a department. Apply it wherever an outcome can be observed, attributed and valued, and be honest about the places where it cannot.

## lowob takeaways

- **Observe it yourself.** The company's own tracking, not the partner's report, confirms the paid-for event.
- **Do not pay the last touch by default.** Stand-down rules and holdouts stop checkout tools collecting for others' work.
- **Define "qualified" in writing.** Hold the definition fixed for the quarter.
- **Track four numbers weekly.** Cost per qualified outcome, approval rate, payback and concentration.

## Common questions

### What is performance marketing?

A way of paying for marketing in which the company pays when a defined outcome happens, such as an account opened or a qualified lead, rather than when an ad is shown. It can apply to affiliate, creator, programmatic and partner channels.

### What is the difference between performance marketing and affiliate marketing?

Affiliate is one channel that runs on performance terms. Performance marketing is the payment standard itself, which also covers creators paid per account, programmatic buys optimised to cost per acquisition and revenue-share partners.

### What metrics should a performance marketing programme track?

Cost per qualified outcome with a written definition, approval rate against the company's own tracking, payback in months and concentration in the top three partners.

### Why is last-click attribution a problem for affiliate programmes?

It pays whoever touched the customer last, which favours coupon sites and browser extensions at checkout. Creators' lawsuits against PayPal's Honey allege an extension overwrote their affiliate cookies this way.
